sessions.name: AI in the Enterprise: A Working Session for Leaders
sessions.desc:
Most organizations aren't short on AI ideas. They're short on clarity about how to turn experimentation into coordinated, trusted, and measurable business performance. 

This three-hour session for business and technical leaders addresses the decisions that actually stall progress: where to focus, what authority AI should have, who owns the outcome, how to manage operational risk, and what must change across governance, technology, and the workforce before an initiative can scale. 

Through real enterprise examples, practical frameworks, and guided exercises, participants will leave with greater clarity around their AI operating model and concrete decisions their leadership team can act on. Facilitated by Phase2.

sessions.name: AI Contract Risk: What Security Professionals Need to Know
sessions.desc:
AI is quickly becoming part of the products and services organizations use every day. This course helps security professionals understand what to look for in contracts when their organization uses AI or when a vendor uses AI to provide services.

The course focuses on practical contract review: what questions to ask, what language should raise concerns, and when security professionals should involve legal, privacy, or other stakeholders.

Key Points:

  • Identifying AI use by vendors and service providers
  • Understanding what data may be shared with AI systems
  • Determining whether organizational data can be used to train or improve AI models
  • Reviewing data ownership, retention, and deletion requirements
  • Understanding AI subprocessors and third-party providers
  • Reviewing security and breach-notification requirements
  • Identifying confidentiality and intellectual-property concerns
  • Addressing vendors that add AI capabilities after a contract is signed
  • Understanding AI opt-in and opt-out provisions
  • Identifying concerning language in contracts, Terms of Service, and privacy policies
  • Knowing what questions security professionals should ask during vendor reviews
  • Knowing when an AI contract issue should be escalated to legal or privacy teams

sessions.name: AI Accountability Workshop
sessions.desc:
Learn how to define clear decision rights, ownership, and guardrails for AI systems so your organization can deploy AI faster, safer, and with unambiguous human accountability.

Learning Objectives

•        Prioritize AI use cases based on value, readiness, and risk

•        Define clear ownership and decision rights for AI initiatives

•        Identify and address governance, ethics, bias, and security risks

•        Know the critical security questions leaders must ask before full deployment

•        Apply key concepts from the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and Generative AI Profile

•        Outline required changes in governance, technology, and workforce

•        Commit to specific next steps their leadership team can take

sessions.name: The Leadership Firewall
sessions.desc:
Technology alone has never been enough to protect an organization. Firewalls, policies, controls, and AI-powered security tools reduce risk, but every system still depends on people making decisions under pressure.

The Leadership Firewall challenges leaders to stop treating people as the weakest link and start developing them as the organization's most adaptive and resilient line of defense. Drawing on two decades in cybersecurity, AI, and highly regulated industries, Melissa Aarskaug reframes five foundational security principles as a practical leadership framework: Know Your Attack Surface, Zero Trust, Defense in Depth, Incident Response, and Patch Yourself.

Attendees leave with the five-part Leadership Firewall framework they can use immediately: identify hidden vulnerabilities, evaluate trust, eliminate single points of failure, prepare for disruption, and replace outdated assumptions before those weaknesses become organizational or personal crises.

sessions.name: One Source of Truth: Why Unified Data Matters (Now More Than Ever)
sessions.desc:
Key Discussion Points:

  • The problem: data chaos is expensive — disjointed data across silos and vendors creates risk and duplication, illustrated by the classic "five different definitions of revenue" problem that erodes trust until people stop using the data.
  • Why unified data is worth it — a single source of truth simplifies data management, reduces vendor reliance, and builds consistency, trust, and lower cost.
  • How it's actually done — a layered approach (raw → governed → consumption) with governance and a semantic layer acting as a shared translator, starting small with clear ownership.
  • Bonus: it sets you up for AI — the same foundation supports reporting, analysis, and AI alike; trustworthy, unified data is most of the work of being "AI ready."

sessions.name: Your AI Model Isn’t the System: Governing Agents, Data, Processes and Outcomes
sessions.desc:
Organizations rarely fail to scale AI because of technology. They fail when pilots encounter production reality: fragmented data, unclear ownership, uncontrolled agent actions, incomplete risk assessments, manual approvals and no credible evidence of business value.

The governance challenge has also moved beyond the model or agent. Modern AI systems combine foundation models, retrieval pipelines, enterprise data, tools, APIs, memory, agents and human decisions. Every component introduces dependencies, failure modes, and accountability questions that traditional model governance was not designed to handle.

Drawing on patterns from enterprise AI and data-value engagements, this session presents a practical operating model for governing AI systems without turning governance into an innovation bottleneck. We will connect business outcomes and risk tiers to concrete production mechanisms: including evaluation gates, system inventories, lineage, tool-access controls, human approvals, runtime monitoring and re-evaluation triggers.

Attendees will learn how to:

·       Frame AI use cases around measurable value and acceptable risk

·       Assign decision rights across business, data, engineering, security, legal, and risk teams

·       Govern agents, models, data, tools and workflows as one system

·       Replace one-time reviews with automated, risk-based lifecycle controls

·       Walk back an AI audit from the business and technical perspective

·       Demonstrate value, reliability, and control using metrics executives will fund

Attendees will leave with a reference operating model and a practical control map for moving AI initiatives from promising pilots to trusted production systems.

sessions.name: Hacked by Your Own AI: Harden Microsoft 365 Before AI Finds the Gaps
sessions.desc:
Organizations are rapidly deploying AI solutions such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude that can access or interact with data in Microsoft 365 (M365), often assuming their existing permissions and security controls are ready for AI. But AI changes the risk equation. Years of oversharing, permission sprawl, weak labeling, and poor governance can suddenly make sensitive information much easier to find, summarize, and expose.

In this session, cybersecurity veteran Geoff Wilson will explain how AI solutions interact with organizational data in M365, where existing security controls can break down, and how attackers may abuse AI-enabled workflows. Attendees will leave with a practical M365 hardening checklist and a roadmap for securely deploying AI solutions that access organizational data.

sessions.name: Data Readiness for AI-Enabled Value Creation
sessions.desc:
Most organizations do not have an AI problem. They have a data readiness problem. As AI becomes embedded into everyday business operations, it quickly exposes issues with data quality, ownership, governance, and process consistency that have existed all along. In this session, Robert Nettles, CISO of Centre Technologies, will provide a practical framework for evaluating whether your organization is truly prepared to create measurable business value from AI. Attendees will learn how to assess data readiness, prioritize high-impact use cases, establish the right governance foundations, and avoid the common mistakes that prevent AI initiatives from delivering meaningful results. The session includes real-world examples, a readiness maturity model, and a practical roadmap for turning AI from a technology experiment into an operational advantage. 

Learning Objectives

  • Evaluate your organization's readiness for AI using a practical framework that measures data quality, ownership, accessibility, governance, and business alignment.
  • Identify and prioritize AI initiatives that deliver measurable business value while avoiding the common data and governance challenges that derail adoption and scale.

sessions.name: Beyond the Hype: Measuring the Real ROI of AI
sessions.desc: AI promises greater efficiency, better decision-making, and transformative innovation, but what happens when the bill comes due? This panel will move beyond the hype to examine how organizations can measure the real return on their AI investments and determine whether AI initiatives are delivering meaningful, sustainable value. Panelists will also address the growing importance of ethical and responsible AI, including governance, transparency, privacy, security, and the human considerations that accompany widespread AI adoption. Finally, as AI demands increasingly strain computing resources, panelists will consider another critical investment decision: cloud, physical data centers, or a hybrid of both? Attendees will gain perspectives on evaluating AI not simply as a technology purchase, but as a broader investment in people, infrastructure, governance, and organizational strategy.

sessions.name: Building Agent Memory with Open Knowledge Format
sessions.desc:
Two engineers recently built knowledge graphs this year on Google's new Open Knowledge Format (OKF), using markdown, git, and AI agents that read from and write back to the graph.

Zach Miller used OKF as the memory layer for a production CRM modernization development effort. Matt Harrison turned the company's scattered knowledge artifacts into a portable cross-departmental graph.  

In this session, you will discover what worked, what didn't, and how to start your own graph better than they did!

What we'll cover:

  • Writing an initial AGENTS.md that tells agents what to create, link, and leave alone
  • Setting up a starting folder structure that lets relationships form naturally
  • Keeping ongoing ingestion from overthinking, overvalidating, and wasting tokens
  • Separating agent-generated knowledge from human-verified knowledge
  • Spotting the signs that a graph costs more than it saves

Who should attend:

This session is for engineers, architects, and technical leads who use AI agents and want them to retain context over time. You should be comfortable with markdown, basic git, and working with AI agents. No graph database experience is needed, and no code will be shown.

sessions.name: A New Way to SIEM: Designing a Distributed Security Data Platform
sessions.desc:
Security teams must detect more, retain data longer, and bring AI into the SOC—all on budgets that lag behind data growth. The traditional monolithic SIEM, which ingests, stores, and detects everything in one system, breaks on cost and flexibility, forcing teams to choose what to collect based on price rather than risk.

A distributed SIEM matches cost to value: each job runs where it's most efficient. A telemetry pipeline shapes, routes, and enriches data before it lands anywhere. A security data lake stores full-fidelity data affordably for retention and investigations. Detection runs only on data that justifies real-time analysis. AI SOC tools work from clean, consistent data for better results—giving you a security program built around your own requirements.

Attendees will learn how to:

·        Design a distributed SIEM around a telemetry pipeline, data lake, and targeted detection

·        Decide what belongs in real-time analytics vs. the lake, and how to retrieve it during investigations

·        Prepare data so AI SOC tools deliver trustworthy triage and investigation results

·        Adopt this architecture in stages alongside an existing SIEM—no rip-and-replace required

sessions.name: Spec-Driven Development: Building Smarter with AI
sessions.desc:
The way we write software is changing — and the developers who thrive won't necessarily be the fastest coders, but the clearest thinkers. Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is a methodology that puts detailed, structured specifications at the center of your workflow, enabling AI coding tools to do the heavy lifting while you focus on architecture, intent, and quality.

In this talk, we'll walk through what SDD looks like in practice: how to write specs that AI tools can actually execute on, and how shifting your planning mindset up front dramatically reduces back-and-forth, hallucinations, and rework. We'll explore how to weave specs directly into your version control pipeline — treating them as living documents that evolve alongside your codebase and serve as a source of truth for both humans and AI alike.

We'll also dig into the power of standardization. When you commit to consistent frameworks, conventions, and tooling, you're not just helping your team — you're dramatically improving the quality and predictability of AI-generated output. AI tools perform best when they have clear patterns to follow, and a standardized stack gives them exactly that.

You'll leave with practical tips and tricks for getting started: how to structure a spec for maximum AI leverage, where SDD fits into your existing Git workflow, and how teams of any size can adopt it incrementally. Whether you're a solo developer or leading an engineering org, Spec-Driven Development offers a path to shipping faster, more consistently, and with greater confidence.

sessions.name: Closing the AI Exposure Window
sessions.desc:
The rate of software vulnerability discovery has been increasing significantly year over year but AI is changing the game. Earlier this year Mythos identified over 20,000 vulnerabilities in code that is the building blocks for most commercial software available today, in just a few hours. It’s not only volume, AI is able to create much more complex exploits that can increase the impact of previously lower severity known issues. Red Hat + IBM recently launched Lightwell to help get you the fixes you need but thats only part of the challenge.

Maintaining your security is paramount, and your ability to do it at machine speed is a necessity. This session explores this new reality and how architecting for automation will allow you to assess, mitigate, consume and verify code fixes at this new pace.

sessions.name: Modernizing Infrastructure for Tomorrow’s Enterprise Network
Identity: The Master Key to Your Data
sessions.desc: The nature of cyberattacks has shifted — attackers now target backup infrastructure directly and increasingly go after identity providers first, since compromising Active Directory, Entra ID, or Okta gives them the keys to everything else. In 2025, roughly 90% of cyberattacks targeted identity providers, yet most organizations still treat identity backup as an afterthought, wrongly assuming Microsoft's shared responsibility model or a 30-day recycle bin is enough. Recovery, not just detection, is what determines whether a ransomware event becomes a headline or a footnote, which is why resilience strategies need to converge data protection and identity recovery into one architecture rather than treating them as separate problems. Rubrik reflects this shift, built on a zero-trust, natively immutable platform that guarantees backups survive an attack on the infrastructure itself, and extends that same recovery guarantee across AD, Entra ID, and Okta so a coordinated ransomware and identity attack can be resolved in hours instead of the weeks a manual forest rebuild typically takes.

·        When the GenAI is wrong and it costs the company something, who owns that?  

·        What “guardrails” have you established for the uses of GenAI?

·        How do you detect “at-home” uses of GenAI?

·        Who is reviewing the outputs of GenAI?

·        Agents are an access problem. Has your identity program caught up with that, or are non-human identities the new service accounts?
